summary: Describes protocol-specific procedures and RSVP-TE extensions for end-to-end recovery of Label Switched Paths in GMPLS networks, covering both protection and restoration. A companion document, RFC 4426, covers the generic functional description. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4872 defines RSVP-TE signaling for recovering an end-to-end GMPLS path after a failure. It describes several ways to arrange backup paths and messages that coordinate switching traffic to a backup and later returning it to the working path.

questions: how does gmpls end-to-end recovery work
what is lsp protection and restoration
what is the rsvp protection object
subtitle: How RSVP-TE identifies protected paths, reserves recovery resources, and coordinates a switch after failure.

tldr.problem: A GMPLS network needs signaling rules for protecting or restoring an end-to-end Label Switched Path after a failure.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4872 extends RSVP-TE with protection and association objects, path information for shared recovery, and Notify procedures for switching and reversion.
tldr.outcome: It defines dedicated protection, shared protection, and rerouting procedures. RFC 4872 updates RFC 3471 and is updated by RFC 4873, RFC 6780, and RFC 9270.

facts.value: Class-Num 199; C-Type 1 for IPv4, 2 for IPv6

today: RFC 4872 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3471. It has been updated by RFC 4873, RFC 6780, and RFC 9270.

sections.title: End-to-End Path Recovery
sections.content:
In this RFC, recovery includes both protection and restoration for a Label Switched Path (LSP) from its head-end to its tail-end. The document specifies procedures for RSVP-TE signaling; RFC 4426 provides a companion functional description. Resource-disjoint paths reduce the chance that one link, node, or shared-risk link group failure affects both the working and protecting LSP.

The RFC covers 1+1 protection, 1:N protection with extra traffic, pre-planned rerouting without extra traffic, and full LSP rerouting. It says the extensions do not affect RSVP-TE Fast Reroute, whose implementations ignore the new objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC describes how the network signals backup paths between the two ends of an LSP. It covers backup paths prepared in advance and routes created after a failure.

sections.title: Working, Protecting, and Secondary LSPs
sections.content:
The PROTECTION object marks an LSP's role and state. The S bit marks a secondary LSP, whose resources are provisioned in the control plane but are not committed in the data plane. The P bit marks a protecting LSP; a working LSP must be primary. The O bit marks a protecting LSP carrying normal traffic after a switch.

The ASSOCIATION object links working and protecting LSPs. On the working LSP, its Association ID identifies the protecting LSP; on the protecting LSP, it identifies the LSP being protected. The two LSPs share the SESSION object and use different LSP IDs.
sections.plainLanguage: Signaling bits say whether a path is working or protecting, whether it is fully active, and whether it carries normal traffic. An association identifier pairs the working path with its backup.

sections.title: Dedicated Protection and Extra Traffic
sections.content:
With 1+1 unidirectional protection, traffic is sent over both fully instantiated LSPs, and the egress chooses the valid path. The endpoints do not coordinate the switch. With 1+1 bidirectional protection, both ends must select the same LSP, so they exchange reliable Notify messages to coordinate the change.

In 1:N protection with extra traffic, a fully provisioned protecting LSP can carry lower-priority extra traffic before it is needed. When a working LSP fails, the endpoints coordinate a switch and disconnect that extra traffic. A single protecting LSP can serve multiple working LSPs between the same endpoints.
sections.plainLanguage: One protection method sends traffic on both paths and lets the receiver choose. Another lets a backup path carry lower-priority traffic, which is disconnected when the backup is needed.

sections.title: Pre-Planned Rerouting and Shared Mesh
sections.content:
For rerouting without extra traffic, the protecting LSP is a secondary path. Its resources can be reserved in the control plane before failure, but it is not ready to carry traffic until activated with additional signaling. The protecting path cannot carry extra traffic while it remains secondary.

Shared-mesh restoration allows protecting LSPs to share recovery resources when the working paths they protect are resource-disjoint. A PRIMARY_PATH_ROUTE object can describe the protected route so an intermediate node can check disjointness. If protected paths overlap, a node SHOULD NOT share the resource and may return a PathErr.
sections.plainLanguage: A backup path can have resources reserved before a failure without being activated. Several backups can share those resources when their working paths do not overlap in the relevant network resources.

sections.title: Preemption, Reversion, and Operator Commands
sections.content:
Other lower-priority LSPs MAY use resources pre-reserved for a secondary protecting LSP. When the protection path activates, those LSPs MUST be preempted. The node releases their resources before sending the new Path message, avoiding a downstream misconnection.

Reversion returns normal traffic to a recovered working LSP. The endpoints coordinate this with Notify messages: the source sends traffic on both paths, requests a switchback, receives confirmation, then completes the change. The RFC also defines commands to lock out a recovery LSP, lock out normal traffic, or request or force a switch.
sections.plainLanguage: When a reserved backup path activates, lower-priority traffic using its resources must give way. After the working path recovers, the endpoints coordinate a return to it.

sections.title: The RSVP-TE Recovery Objects
sections.content:
The PROTECTION object carries status bits and a protection-type flag. Defined types include full rerouting, rerouting without extra traffic, 1:N protection with extra traffic, and 1+1 unidirectional or bidirectional protection. A node unable to meet the requested protection type MUST send a PathErr indicating unsupported LSP protection.

The PRIMARY_PATH_ROUTE object lists subobjects copied from the protected path, such as an IPv4 address, IPv6 address, label, or unnumbered interface. The ASSOCIATION object includes an association type, association ID, and source address. The RFC adds these objects to RSVP Path and Resv message formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Three objects describe the recovery arrangement: one marks the protection type, one can list the protected route, and one pairs the paths. RSVP Path messages carry the relevant information to nodes along the route.

sections.title: Security and IANA Assignments
sections.content:
RSVP signaling MUST provide authentication and integrity so nodes can verify message origin and detect changes in transit. The RFC points to RSVP message authentication for hop-by-hop exchanges and IPsec-based authentication and integrity for exchanges that are not hop-by-hop, including Notify messages.

The new objects, error values, and ADMIN_STATUS bits need shared assignments. The RFC defines Lockout as the ADMIN_STATUS bit at position 26 and assigns recovery-related RSVP error code and sub-code values.
sections.plainLanguage: Switching messages need authentication and integrity so a node can trust their source and contents. The RFC assigns common numbers to the new recovery objects and error conditions.
